questions.q: Why does it make sense to run task nodes on Spot Instances but keep core nodes on-demand?
options: Task nodes hold no HDFS data, so losing one to Spot reclamation only costs recomputation; core nodes hold HDFS data, so losing one risks data loss
Spot Instances are not available for any node type in EMR
Core nodes are always cheaper than task nodes regardless of pricing model
There is no meaningful difference — either node type is equally safe on Spot
questions.explain: The data-safety distinction between core (stores HDFS data) and task (compute only) nodes is exactly why Spot fits task nodes but is risky for core nodes.

questions.q: What is an EMR instance fleet?
options: A configuration allowing a mix of instance types and purchase options within a node role, with EMR choosing what's available at launch
A fixed single instance type applied to every node role
A separate EMR product unrelated to clusters
A billing construct with no effect on which instances actually launch
questions.explain: Instance fleets (as opposed to single-type instance groups) let EMR select from a set of eligible instance types/purchase options, useful for improving Spot availability.

questions.q: What does EMR's managed scaling typically use as the metric driving task node count?
options: Workload-demand metrics like YARN's memory or container-pending metrics, reflecting actual queued work
The time of day only, regardless of actual workload
The AWS account's total monthly budget
The number of S3 buckets in the account
questions.explain: Managed scaling policies react to real demand signals such as YARN memory availability, not a fixed schedule, adding/removing task nodes within a configured min/max.

questions.q: Which EC2 instance family is best suited to a Spark job that shuffles large amounts of data in memory?
options: Memory-optimized (r family)
Compute-optimized (c family) exclusively, in every case
Storage-optimized instances only, never memory-optimized
Instance family choice has no effect on Spark job performance
questions.explain: Memory-optimized instances (the r family) are the natural fit for shuffle-heavy Spark workloads that need large in-memory capacity.

questions.q: What bounds does a managed scaling policy set for task node count?
options: A minimum and maximum instance count, within which EMR adjusts automatically
Only a maximum, with no minimum ever enforced
A fixed exact count that never changes
Managed scaling policies apply only to core nodes, never task nodes
questions.explain: A managed scaling policy defines a min/max range, and EMR scales the task node count within those bounds as workload demand changes.
